item.title: Mathematical modeling to study combination strategies for neural stem cell therapy in glioblastoma
item.description: arXiv:2611.01374v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Neural stem cells (NSCs) are a promising treatment platform due to their ability to cross the restrictive blood-brain barrier and migrate toward damaged regions of the brain. These properties can be leveraged to target brain tumors, as NSCs can infiltrate tumor lesions and deliver therapeutic agents such as drugs, oncolytic viruses, and genetic materials. Despite the advantages of NSCs, translational challenges remain, including patient-specific chemotactic signaling and immune responses, variability in migration and localization at tumor sites, and optimization of delivery strategies. In this work, we focus on intranasal delivery of NSCs and combination strategies for the treatment of brain cancer. To investigate strategies for improving NSC arrival at the tumor site, we developed a hybrid mathematical model of NSC migration that couples an agent-based model with a partial differential equation, where cell motion is guided by the spatial dynamics of chemoattractants. Using data collected from a murine model and our mathematical model, we {investigate treatment-motivated downstream effects associated with three combination strategies:} (1) IL-10 pretreatment, (2) CXCL12 pretreatment, and (3) radiotherapy. We find that IL-10 pretreatment improves NSC arrival numbers at tumor only under the Gaussian chemoattractant profile, whereas CXCL12 pretreatment moderately improves arrival numbers when the tumor is located in the anterior brain. Radiotherapy significantly enhances the tumor arrival under uniform profiles. These simulation studies suggest that both treatment strategies and chemoattractant distribution influence intranasal NSC delivery, and the proposed model can be used to predict how targeted modulation of chemotactic signaling and tissue-guided migration may improve delivery outcomes.
item.dc:creator: Ashley Harrison, Austin Hansen, Anthony E. Bishay, Greg Grigoryan, Vikram Adhikarla, Russell C. Rockne, Margarita Gutova, Heyrim Cho

item.title: The Kinetic Basis of the Genetic Code
item.description: arXiv:2611.01832v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The origin of the genetic code is an enigma, requiring explanations for the emergence of degeneracy, the organizational structure of the code, and the correspondence between codons and amino acids. Here, we use the asymmetric cooperativity model to show that these features arise from asymmetric cooperativity in codon-anticodon association process. We first provide mechanistic and evolutionary accounts of wobble base pair degeneracy, without providing any preferential treatment to the third position. The model, with four tunable parameters, reproduces the organizational structure of the genetic code, and provides theoretical codon-anticodon association times. Although ribosomal kinetic data are not used in parameter estimation, these theoretical association times correlate with experimentally determined ribosomal residence times (r=0.73). The resulting timescales, extending over four decades, also exhibit correlations with diverse physicochemical properties of amino acids, at multiple timescales, motivating a nonequilibrium picture in which energy released during codon-anticodon association is transferred to its cognate amino acid to be dissipated into water. Finally, without incorporating information about aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases or further parameter adjustment, the model recovers the division of amino acids associated with the two aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase classes, with a combined segregation score of 0.92 ( p~10^{-8}). These results suggest that wobble degeneracy, genetic-code organization, translation kinetics, amino-acid physicochemistry, and the two-class organization of aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases may reflect a common underlying kinetic constraint. We propose that non-equilibrium, asymmetrically cooperative kinetics, that possibly underlie DNA/RNA replication process, also provided a physical basis upon which the genetic code and its subsequent translation machinery evolved.
